newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Non-aligned reject ILO bid for tougher job role.
newsitem.headline: Non-aligned reject ILO bid for tougher job role.

text.p: Nearly 120 developing countries, backed by China, on Wednesday rejected a bid by the chief of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) to give the body a stronger hand in curbing abuse of workers around the world.
They also condemned his proposal, backed by Western countries and trade unions, to move towards a system of "social labelling" of goods produced in conformity with ILO core labour standards.
They told the United Nations agency's annual conference the proposal amounted to legitimising trade protectionism.
The emerging economies set out their position, endorsed by their labour ministers, in a statement read by Colombia on behalf of 113 members of the non-aligned movement (NAM) and five others.

It said the approach and argumentation of a report to the conference by ILO Director-General Michel Hansenne was "inherently flawed" and introduced "an untenable link between labour standards and trade which we do not accept."

In a further rebuke to Hansenne, a former Belgian social affairs minister, it said the body -- oldest in the U.N. system -- should instead be helping developing countries facing "protectionist pressures in the context of labour standards".
There is a long-running global argument over "trade and labour" which generally runs on North versus South lines but also divides labour unions in developing countries and governments in the West.

After efforts led by the United States and France to put the issue on the agenda of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) failed last year, the WTO's Ministerial Meeting in Singapore last December passed it back to the ILO.

Hansenne, who is due to step down in 1999, seized the opportunity to launch a campaign to obtain more powers for the ILO to check how far countries were translating economic development resulting from freer trade into social progress.

He also sought support from the 173 members of the Geneva-based body for drafting a declaration of fundamental rights that would in effect bind them to observe core labour standards, whether their legislature had ratified them or not.

These standards include freedom of association -- or the right to set up independent trade unions -- and collective bargaining, banning of forced labour and child labour, equality of treatment for women and non-discrimination between workers.

International trade union bodies based in the West, who play a major role in the workers' group in the tripartite structure of the ILO, support these ideas, as do some labour groupings in emerging economies.

The Brussels-based World Confederation of Labour (WCL), which has many developing country members, said in a report on Wednesday that economic globalisation on market principles had brought a sharp rise in violation of workers' rights.
Presenting the report at a Geneva news conference, WCL Secretary-General Willy Thys singled out Indonesia -- a prominent member of the non-aligned movement -- as one of the major violators.

The larger International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), also based in Brussels and which earlier campaigned for a trade-and-labour link in the WTO, is issuing a similar report later this week in which emerging economies figure large.

But in their statement, the NAM states said the ILO should be helping countries facing such pressure "to clarify their commitments to uphold labour standards in conformity with their obligations and respective levels of development."
China, although only an observer in the non-aligned movement, put its name to the statement. Chile, Jamaica, South Africa and Venezuela said they supported it, but with reservations.
